source_read: PDF pp. 1-7 (all pages; Tables 2 and 3 checked on the rendered page, Table 2's confidence-interval column on a zoomed render). Paragraph numbering on p. 4 was re-checked on a zoomed render after step 2: the 7th Results paragraph continues across the column break, so the behaviour and acceptability paragraphs are the 8th and 9th. Three of the blind locators were corrected accordingly, with no change to data or verdicts.

claims.note: Recomputed: 217/336 = 64.6%, 86/336 = 25.6% (Wilson 21.2-30.5%), 6/336 = 1.8% (Wilson 0.8-3.8%); same as the claim. The 336 are answers on returned sheets from 218 people (some answered more than once); the paper calls them participants. The categories sum to 309, so 27 answers are not accounted for. The most common safer answer was using less or more slowly (45); not using at all was 7 (2.1%, editors' calculation). This fits 'most often using less or going slower, and seldom' not using; the paper's category is not using at all, with no separate category for throwing away. The questions were standard ones about potential results (Methods), and the authors say answers may be hypothetical or actual (Discussion), so 'what they did' is the survey's framing, not observed behaviour; the claim says so. The abstract gives 27% and frames it as 'when fentanyl was detected', which overstates; the claim rightly uses the Results figure.

anchors.extracted: Asked what they did if a drug tested positive: no change 217 (64.6%); at least one safer change 86 (25.6%): use less or more slowly 45, use with someone else 26, use at an overdose prevention or supervised consumption site 9, not use at all 7, someone checks on them 4 (multiple answers allowed); riskier 6 (1.8%): 1 using more or faster, 5 using alone.

anchors.locator: Methods › Survey tools and testing kits, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Survey at return asked about actions after both a positive and a negative result; questions were standard ones about potential results, not based on the strips returned; multiple answers allowed; CAD 5 honorarium.

Behaviour questions were open to interpretation, so answers could be hypothetical or about an actual result; each sheet held five results, so behaviour could not be linked to substance; the sample was not random.
Abstract: 27% reported a safer change when fentanyl was detected; this differs from 25.6% (86/336) in the Results and presents standard-question answers as responses to detection.

claims.overstatement: 'at home' is narrower than the source: take-home strips were used at home on 54.8% of sheets, in alleys or streets on 22.0% and at supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites on 28.9% (p. 4). 'With take-home strips' would be accurate.
claims.note: Recomputed: 6/336 = 1.8% (Wilson 0.8-3.8%), 1 more or faster and 5 alone: same. Responses to a negative result were asked (Methods) and not reported: confirmed. Positivity: 73/265 = 27.5% (the paper prints 27.6%, a rounding slip; 28 in 100 either way), 5/97 = 5.2%, 16/93 = 17.2%, 1/92 = 1.1%; differences 22.4 points (14.7 to 30.1 by a Wald interval with continuity correction; paper 14.8 to 30.1) and 16.1 (7.1 to 25.2; paper 25.1): same within rounding. The authors judge a testing-method explanation (false positives when too little dilution is used, instructions possibly not followed) more likely than differently contaminated supplies: confirmed. Two qualifiers the claim could use: training stressed possible false negatives and that strips do not detect all adulterants (p. 2), a step against false reassurance; and 3.3% (p. 3) or 3.8% (p. 4) of strips gave unclear results, after which what people did is unknown.

claims.note: 322/336 = 95.8% (recomputed: same) said they would use strips again; an intention, as the claim says. The 336 are answers from 218 people: 118 sheets (editors' calculation) were returned by people who had returned one before, a behavioural sign that some participants took further kits within the four months. The paper does not report how many people returned more than once, and kits not returned were not followed up.

claims.note: Counts recomputed as for cl_dc_caution_harms (73/265 = 27.5%, printed 27.6%). The authors' false-positive reasoning rests partly on a trend with experience (first-time to experienced testers: crystal methamphetamine 28.9% to 15.2%, cocaine 28.3% to 7.8%, p. 4; the text does not say whether these are positivity or take-home minus on-site differences, and either way take-home stays above on-site), and the paper's experience comparison for opioids is internally inconsistent (Table 3: 78.4% positive for experienced testers with p = 0.24 printed, while these counts against first-time testers' 90.7% give p < 0.001; the text says the gap from on-site shrank to 0.6 points). Missed second-hand figure: the paper relays specificity 95.2% (and sensitivity 87.5%) for the same strips from a validation study (Ti et al., 2020; p. 2).

anchors.extracted: Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 take-home against 5/97 on site; cocaine 16/93 against 1/92; different samples, aggregate comparison, not powered for stimulants.

Testing method judged the more likely explanation: false positives with stimulants when too little dilution is used; instructions possibly not followed; further education and substance-specific instructions suggested.

By experience with strips: opioid gap from on-site 1.6 points for first-time and 0.6 for experienced testers; crystal methamphetamine 28.9% to 15.2% and cocaine 28.3% to 7.8% (not stated whether positivity or differences); offered as support for the testing-method explanation.
BTNX urine strips used off-label on diluted drug; relayed detection limit 130 ng/mL and sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 95.2% (Ti et al., 2020, second-hand); strips cannot quantify.

Where take-home strips were used (sheets, more than one setting possible): home, including private residences, tents and single-room hotels, 184 (54.8%); alleys and streets 74 (22.0%); overdose prevention or supervised consumption sites 97 (28.9%).

claims.overstatement: Minor: 'No sample was tested both at home and on site'. The design did not pair samples, but participants could also use on-site checking, so overlap cannot be excluded; 'no sample was tested both ways by design' is what the paper supports. The claim could name the single brand (BTNX), used in both arms.
claims.note: Counts and percentages recomputed: 994/1105 = 90.0% (the Results text prints 89.9%), 591/663 = 89.1%, difference 0.8 points (-2.3 to 3.9, reproduced by a Wald interval with continuity correction; TOST p = 0.00275; Table 2 also prints p = 0.59 for the difference); crystal methamphetamine 73/265 = 27.5% (printed 27.6%) against 5/97 = 5.2%; cocaine 16/93 = 17.2% against 1/92 = 1.1%: same. 218 people, 336 sheets, ten sites, April-July 2019: confirmed. Recall: Table 3 has 122 completed and 206 recalled sheets (206/328 = 62.8%; 689 of 1074 opioid results, 64.2%), the text the reverse: confirmed. Kits handed out and not returned: not followed up, and no number is reported: confirmed. The authors' conclusion that people can use strips 'accurately ... with minimal training' (p. 4): confirmed. Qualifiers the claim does not state: (1) take-home strips were used at home on 54.8% of sheets, in alleys or streets on 22.0% and at supervised sites on 28.9%; (2) the comparator was also strip testing, by trained peer workers and technicians, not a laboratory method; (3) the abstract says results were not affected by experience with strips, but Table 3 shows 78.4% positivity in experienced testers' opioid results (116/148) against 90.7% for first-time testers (508/560), with a printed p = 0.24 that these counts do not give (chi-squared about 17, p < 0.001, editors' calculation); the text's 0.6-point gap from on-site does not fit 78.4% (that gap would be about -10.8 points), so the experienced row is internally inconsistent; (4) unclear results are given as 3.3% (p. 3) and 3.8% (p. 4).

anchors.extracted: 852 samples tested on site (663 believed opioid, 189 stimulant); opioid positivity 89.9% take-home against 89.1% on site, difference 0.81% (95% CI -2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within the pre-set 5 points, p = 0.00275.

Cross-sectional comparison of aggregate positivity; equivalence margin 5 percentage points; 617 samples per group needed; four months gave too few stimulant samples; results self-reported and no confirmatory analyses.

Table 3: completed sheets n = 122 (385 opioid results), recalled n = 206 (689); the text gives recalled n = 122 and completed n = 206. Experienced testers: 116/148 (78.4%) positive against first-time 508/560 (90.7%), p printed 0.24.

Authors: opioid results concordant, suggesting people who use drugs can use strips accurately with minimal training where they choose; stimulants may differ in reliability; no restrictions on place or method of use.
Stimulant excess: testing method judged more likely than different supplies; dilution instructions possibly not followed.

No demographic data on people using on-site checking; assumed no systematic difference between the samples of the two groups; no design in which the same sample was tested by a person and by an expert; the same sample may have been tested repeatedly with a kit's five strips.

key_findings.note: Recomputed: 994/1105 = 89.95%, 591/663 = 89.14%; the interval is reproduced by a Wald interval with continuity correction (-2.26 to 3.89).
73/265 is 27.5% (printed 27.6%); immaterial. Cocaine p = 0.0048 matches neither chi-square (0.00015; 0.0004 with continuity correction) nor Fisher's exact test (0.00015) (editors' calculations).

The paper does not say whether the stimulant figures (28.9% to 15.2%; 28.3% to 7.8%) are positivity or take-home minus on-site differences. 'Differences' is the likelier reading, because the sentence follows the opioid differences.
The other three p-values match uncorrected chi-square tests on the printed counts (0.66, 0.36, 0.68); experience gives chi-square 17.0, p < 0.001 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: chi-square 17.0, p < 0.001; 148/153 = 0.97 opioid results per sheet against 560/173 = 3.24.

The reversal between text and table is confirmed, but the 610-result check does not show that the table is right. If the text is right, the table's row labels (not its n) are swapped: the 122 sheets would be the recalled ones, holding 385 results (at most 610, so possible), and the 206 completed sheets would hold 689. Both versions fit the counts, so which is right is unknown. 'About 63% of sheets from recall' holds by Table 3 only, which is how cl_dc_home_vs_service words it.

The abstract's sentence follows the opioid result and agrees with the Results' own statement that prior experience was not associated with positivity (4th paragraph, p. 4; Table 3). For opioids, the trend in the 6th paragraph stays within the equivalence margin (1.6 and 0.6 points). The real conflicts are with Table 3's experienced row (issue 0) and with the stimulant trend, which the abstract's sentence does not address.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall serious agreed, and the domain judgments too. ROBINS-I is a defensible choice for comparing two ways of delivering testing. With no reference method and no paired samples, this is not a test-accuracy study under METHODS §5.3, so QUADAS-2 does not apply; the positivity descriptions could also be read with the JBI prevalence checklist. The validator's design-instrument warning needs the editor's sign-off.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed: 'accurately' and 'reliability' are claimed from positivity on different, unconfirmed samples. One correction to the 'claimed' text: the abstract's statement that experience did not affect results refers to the opioid results and matches the Results' 4th paragraph (see the check of reporting issue index 3).

missed: Table 2 rounding: 73/265 is 27.5% (printed 27.6%, repeated in key finding 5 and analysis.effect_sizes) and 92/97 is 94.8% (printed 94.9%).

336 sheets from 218 people imply 118 repeat returns (editors' calculation), a behavioural sign that some participants took further kits within the four months; how many people returned more than once is not reported. Relevant to cl_dc_continued_use.

design_detail and cannot_establish say that no sample was tested both ways. The paper shows only that the design did not pair samples; participants could also use on-site checking, so overlap cannot be excluded (as selection_effects says).

Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 5): the authors say growing evidence suggests strips may help prevent overdose, citing Peiper 2019. Kutscher et al. (2024) include Peiper 2019 (their ref. 38) but find only two studies with overdose outcomes (their refs 69 and 81), so that citation does not show overdose prevention. This is an interpretation-gap item.
